Variance Conventions of a Fit

Source: R/inference_objects.R
vcov_method.Rd

Three conventions set the variance matrix of the coefficients of a fit: the Bayesian one, the frequentist one and the unconditional one. Each is an object built by bayesian_vcov(), frequentist_vcov() or unconditional_vcov(), and the object is passed as the argument vcov_type of vcov.StatmodFit(), confint.StatmodFit(), summary.StatmodFit(), statmod_test() and predict.StatmodFit(). The default is bayesian_vcov().

vcov_method is the abstract parent of the three classes. It cannot be instantiated, and serves to test membership with S7::S7_inherits(). It has the property name only. The three conventions of this topic compute the variance from the curvature of the likelihood and carry one more property, information, which selects the matrix \(H\) (see below). A convention that does not read the curvature, such as bootstrap_vcov(), which is the covariance of refitted, resampled data sets, does not carry it.

Usage

vcov_method(name = character(0))

Arguments

name

A single string, the short name of the convention ("bayesian", "frequentist" or "unconditional"), which is also the stem of the constructor (bayesian_vcov() and so on). A result prints it.

Value

Nothing: the class is abstract and its constructor signals an error. Every object that inherits from it has the property name; the three conventions of this topic have the property information as well.

Details

Write \(H\) for the information of the log-likelihood and \(S\) for the second derivative of the penalty, both at the estimates. The argument information of bayesian_vcov(), frequentist_vcov() and unconditional_vcov() selects \(H\): NULL (the default), which is resolved for each fit by the family, distributions7::observed_info(), the negative Hessian of the log-likelihood at the data, or distributions7::expected_info(), the Fisher information, with a method that selects how the expectation is obtained. The default is the observed information where the log-likelihood is twice differentiable in every parameter of the family (every distributions7::params_order() is at least 2), and the expected information, for the whole matrix, otherwise: a family such as the Laplace has a singular observed information in its location, and the closed form of the expected information gives finite standard errors. auto_info() is not accepted, since the variance is defined on one named matrix. summary.StatmodFit() states the matrix whenever it is not the observed one, and a printed variance object states the information that it names. The effective degrees of freedom that summary.StatmodFit() prints are read on the same matrix. The choice is independent of the information with which the fit was computed (inner_information of statmod()) and of the one of the outer criterion (the information of reml()). A model that carries a structural term is inverted on the observed information whatever the object says. The three matrices are $$V_b = (H + S)^{-1}, \qquad V_f = (H+S)^{-1} H (H+S)^{-1}, \qquad V' = V_b + J V_\theta J'.$$

  • bayesian_vcov() returns \(V_b\), the posterior variance under the prior whose negative logarithm is the penalty, conditional on the hyperparameters. It carries the smoothing bias as variance, so an interval around a penalized term built from it covers at about its nominal rate.

  • frequentist_vcov() returns \(V_f\), the sandwich: the sampling variance of the penalized estimator at a fixed penalty. It is smaller than \(V_b\) and covers less.

  • unconditional_vcov() returns \(V'\). The first two matrices read the hyperparameters (smoothing parameters, variances of random effects, scales of a prior) at the value where the outer search stopped, as though that value were known. \(V'\) adds the variance that their estimation contributes, with \(V_\theta\) the variance of the estimated hyperparameters on their own free scale and \(J = -(H + S)^{-1}\,\partial^2\rho/\partial\beta\,\partial\theta\) the movement of the penalized mode under them (Wood, Pya and Safken, 2016). The correction is positive semi-definite, so \(V'\) is never narrower than \(V_b\). It requires the curvature of the outer criterion, which the other two do not read, and it is the most expensive of the three.

With no penalty \(S = 0\) and \(V_b\) and \(V_f\) are both \(H^{-1}\) for a coefficient that the outer criterion does not estimate. Where the observed information is singular at the estimates, as it is for a coefficient on which the second derivative of the log-likelihood is zero (the location of a Laplace response), the rows of the coefficients that it does not identify are missing. The default NULL reads the expected information for such a family, which is finite there. Where no hyperparameter was estimated by a differentiable criterion the correction of the unconditional matrix is zero and it equals \(V_b\). The coefficients that reml() and ml() estimate on the criterion (the unpenalized coefficients of every parameter but the first, by default) take the curvature of that criterion under the Bayesian and the unconditional conventions, which therefore differ from the frequentist one for them even without a penalty. The complete description of the matrices, of the coordinates that are held and of the warnings is at vcov.StatmodFit().

References

Wood, S. N., Pya, N. and Safken, B. (2016). Smoothing parameter and model selection for general smooth models. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 111(516), 1548–1563.

See also

bayesian_vcov(), frequentist_vcov() and unconditional_vcov() for the three conventions, vcov.StatmodFit() for the matrices, test_statistic for the tests that read a variance.

Examples

set.seed(1)
ds <- data.frame(x = runif(200))
ds$y <- sin(2 * pi * ds$x) + rnorm(200, sd = 0.3)
fs <- statmod(y ~ s(x, bspline_smooth(k = 10)),
              distributions7::gaussian1_distrib(), ds)

# the standard error of one penalized coordinate under each convention
types <- list(frequentist_vcov(), bayesian_vcov(), unconditional_vcov())
vapply(types, function(ty) {
  sqrt(diag(vcov(fs, vcov_type = ty)))[["mu:s(x).z2"]]
}, numeric(1))
#> [1] 0.06053712 0.06083113 0.06134753

# the matrix H is chosen inside the convention
sqrt(diag(vcov(fs, vcov_type = bayesian_vcov(
  information = distributions7::expected_info()))))[["mu:s(x).z2"]]
#> [1] 0.06081721

# the class itself is abstract
try(vcov_method(name = "mine"))
#> Error in S7::new_object(S7::S7_object(), name = name) : 
#>   Can't construct an object from abstract class <vcov_method>
